newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil stocks seen unhurt by U.S. Fed rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Brazil stocks seen unhurt by U.S. Fed rate rise.

text.p: Brazil's stock market is unlikely to suffer from a rise in U.S. interest rates after the Federal Reserve raised funds rates by 25 basis points as widely expected, analysts said.

"The impact of the quarter percentage point increase has already been fully priced in," said Clive Botelho, executive director at Sao Paulo-based Banco BMG. "A correction in prices has already taken place." Last week, Brazilian shares lost two percent on U.S. stock and bond volatility ahead of today's Federal Reserve Open Market (FOMC) meeting.
But selling pressure eased on Monday after Wall Street signalled it had absorbed the rate increase.
Botelho said the local market already opened this morning with the sentiment the Fed would raise rates by only 25 basis points, rising over one percent earlier.
Sergio Goldman, head of Research at Banco Santander's Brazil unit, believes the impact of the rate rise on the Brazilian stock exchange will be minimal to none.
"Brazil has so many other factors to look to such as privatizations, reforms that the rate hike ends up being a secondary issue," he said.
Goldman said positive prospects for Brazil's privatizations should keep foreign investors interested in the local bolsa.
"The rate hike is unlikely to be a reason to slow foreign inflows," he said.

Foreign buys were behind much of this year's rally. Net capital inflows to Brazilian bourses under Annex Four rules totalled $1.698 billion in January and February, almost half of last year's total net foreign inflows of $3.593 billion.

Brazil is set to auction a 45 percent stake in mining conglomerate Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) on April 29 and is about to privatise its telecommunications sector with the auctions of Band B cellular concessions.
Some experts also said the 25 basis point rise calmed the markets as the FOMC was in step with Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's recent remarks.
"After Greenspan's several warnings on the U.S. economy, he had to do something," said Odair Abate, chief economist at Lloyds Bank, Brazil.
"Now the market will be free to follow other factors."
